message.reasoning:
I need to write a JUnit 4 test class for joda-time's DateTimeFormatter, covering as many branches as I can analyze, using only JUnit4 and joda-time classes since the target code requires it.

I'm planning test cases for the constructor, getPrinter/getParser, withLocale, getLocale, withOffsetParsed, withChronology, withZoneUTC/withZone, withPivotYear (both Integer and int overloads), getPivotYear, withDefaultYear, getDefaultYear, and printTo with various instant handling branches including the null-instant case that falls back to current time.

I'm also covering the printTo overloads for Writer, Appendable, longs, ReadablePartial (including the null-partial exception case), the requirePrinter failure path, and the print() convenience methods. I'm thinking through how to trigger the overflow branch in the private printTo method, which requires constructing an instant near Long.MAX_VALUE with a zone offset that causes a sign overflow when adjusted.

This confirms the existing logic correctly falls back to UTC without throwing, though formatting Long.MAX_VALUE afterward could still trigger a separate year-out-of-range exception when converting with the UTC chronology.

Actually even without the offset, Long.MAX_VALUE milliseconds translates to a year far beyond ISO chronology's maximum (~292,278,994), so the year calculation itself would overflow and throw before the offset ever comes into play.

Given how entangled this is with real printer implementations, I think the cleanest approach is a stub DateTimePrinter that captures the arguments passed to printTo, letting me verify directly that UTC zone, zero offset, and the unadjusted instant get passed through on overflow—covering both the overflow and normal branches without depending on a real formatter succeeding. I need to check what methods the DateTimePrinter interface requires so I can implement a minimal stub.

Implementing a custom stub printer feels overly complex, so it's probably simpler to just use real formatters like ISODateTimeFormat.dateTime() and skip the extreme overflow edge case, noting that branch isn't fully covered since it needs unrealistic big longs that cause chronology range errors.

But since maximum branch coverage matters, I want to try a custom stub printer to indirectly exercise the private method through print(long) and printTo(StringBuffer, long), testing the overflow branch with instant=Long.MAX_VALUE and default ISO chronology.

Adding Long.MAX_VALUE always overflows when combined with any positive offset, so I don't need an extreme offset value, just a positive one. Since relying on the system's default time zone offset is unreliable across machines, I should explicitly set the zone using withZone and a fixed positive offset like +2 hours to guarantee the overflow condition triggers deterministically.

Using a real printer like ISODateTimeFormat.dateTime() at that point would likely throw an exception internally since calculating year from Long.MAX_VALUE millis can overflow or raise a field value error. Since the test only needs to cover the branch, not verify correct output, I can just assert that calling with this input throws some RuntimeException.

I'll settle on using expected=Exception.class as a safe, generic catch for the boundary test, since I don't want to guess at the exact exception type the overflow would trigger and should stick strictly to what the source code actually guarantees.

The no-overflow branch is already implicitly covered by normal print(long) usage without zone overrides. I should also directly exercise the Writer variant of printTo, since it duplicates the StringBuffer logic in a separate private method, calling it once for the normal case and once for the overflow case to get full coverage.

Now I'm settling on real formatter combinations to use: ISODateTimeFormat.dateTime() as a full printer+parser, plus constructing parser-only and printer-only DateTimeFormatter instances by extracting the underlying printer/parser from that same formatter.

With those in hand, I'm sketching out the test cases: verifying both-null construction yields isPrinter/isParser false, verifying printer-only and parser-only construction set the flags correctly, checking the combined formatter has both, and testing withLocale behavior—returning the same instance when passed null (matching default locale) versus creating a new instance for a different locale.

I'm continuing to outline withLocale tests for repeated and differing locales, then moving to withOffsetParsed, checking that it transitions false to true on first call, returns the same instance on subsequent identical calls, and setting up further variations of that pattern.

Next I'm verifying that withOffsetParsed() also resets the zone to null even after withZone was previously called, confirming that behavior against the source logic before moving on to withChronology, checking that passing null returns the same instance when the default chronology is already null.

Then I'm testing withChronology with an actual ISOChronology instance to confirm it returns a new formatter with that chronology set, and that passing the same chronology reference again returns the identical object due to reference equality.

Finally I'm checking withZoneUTC(), confirming it sets the zone to UTC and always resets offsetParsed to false regardless of the prior state, since the implementation unconditionally passes false.

Next I'm testing withZone with null (returns the same instance when both zones are null), with a specific zone like Europe/Paris (creates a new formatter with that zone set), and confirming that calling withZone again with the same zone reference returns the same instance.

Since the equality check uses reference comparison rather than value equality, I need to verify that two separately obtained but equal DateTimeZone instances for the same ID don't necessarily trigger the "return this" shortcut unless they're cached as the same object reference.

I also need to cover withPivotYear behavior: passing a null pivotYear when it's already null should return this, assigning a new value creates a new instance with that value, and even passing an equal Integer value should still produce a different object since Integer isn't interned at that range.

For withDefaultYear, I'm verifying it updates getDefaultYear() correctly from the default of 2000. Then I move toward testing print methods, starting with a basic ReadableInstant print using an ISO formatter against a UTC DateTime.

For null instants, I'm checking that print falls back to current time via DateTimeUtils without throwing, so just asserting a non-null, non-empty result. For the long-based print, I need a UTC-explicit formatter since the default zone varies across test environments, then verify printing epoch millis (0L) gives the expected 1970-01-01 string.

For testing partial printing, I realize the full dateTime() formatter requires time fields it won't find on a LocalDate, which could throw an exception, so I should use a date-only formatter instead to safely test printTo on a ReadablePartial.

I'm sketching out tests covering null-partial checks for printTo with StringBuffer and Writer, successful printing of a LocalDate through both, and verifying Appendable-based printing works correctly for partials, instants, and longs.

I'm also noting tests confirming that a parser-only formatter throws UnsupportedOperationException when asked to print, and a printer-only formatter throws the same when asked to parse. Then I move into parsing tests, checking that a valid ISO string parses to the correct millisecond value while an invalid string throws an exception.

I'm also adding a case for strings with trailing junk that cause an incomplete parse, which should throw IllegalArgumentException, plus tests confirming parseLocalDate and parseLocalTime correctly extract the expected date and time values.

For the time-only test, I'll avoid ambiguity around default zone offsets by using ISODateTimeFormat.hourMinuteSecondMillis(), which parses "HH:mm:ss.SSS" without requiring a zone, pairing it with ISODateTimeFormat.date() for the date-only case.

I'm now drafting tests for parsing LocalDateTime, verifying that incomplete input throws, and confirming that DateTime parsed against UTC matches the expected millis value.

I'm also checking withOffsetParsed behavior to ensure the parsed offset zone is preserved correctly, then testing a zone override case where the formatter is explicitly set to UTC.

Now I need another test to hit the branch where bucket.getZone() is non-null rather than the offset integer—this happens when the pattern includes a textual zone name field like 'zzz' instead of a numeric offset 'Z', so I should use DateTimeFormat with that pattern.

I'm also outlining remaining test cases: invalid input throwing exceptions, partial-not-full matches throwing, MutableDateTime parsing variants (normal, invalid, zone override), and parseInto tests that verify the returned position and resulting millis, plus a null-instant case that should throw.

For parseInto, I'm covering offset-parsed branches, zone override application after parsing, and the case where invalid text returns a negative position rather than throwing. Finally, I'm noting that selectChronology gets indirect coverage through the chronology override tests already planned via print/parse, with both iChrono null and non-null cases needing checks.

Given the scope is already large, I'll prioritize solid branch coverage while flagging uncertain behaviors like zone-versus-chronology precedence and named zone parsing as comments rather than fully testing every edge case, then move to finalize the test code.

I also want to exercise the two-arg and instant-based printTo overloads to ensure they delegate properly through the chronology-null paths. For the test file, I'll need the standard Joda imports plus JUnit assertions, and I'll wrap the overflow-branch test in a try-catch to confirm it compiles and runs without asserting a specific failure.

Since I'm uncertain about the exact overflow behavior for Long.MAX_VALUE, I'll avoid guessing the precise exception type and instead just verify that some exception is thrown, documenting that uncertainty in a comment rather than asserting a specific subtype.

So the exception should surface regardless of whether the revert happened. I should also confirm that normal prints at moderate long values, like 0 or current time, don't throw—that's already covered by the no-overflow default tests where offset is zero. I still need a case with a nonzero offset but no overflow to properly exercise the else branch where offset differs from zero without triggering the overflow condition.

I'll add a test using a formatter with a +5 hour offset zone printing epoch 0, expecting "1970-01-01T05:00:00.000+05:00", which exercises the non-overflow path with a nonzero offset going straight to printTo. I'll mirror this test for the Writer-based printTo overload too, then move on to writing the actual test code, assuming org.joda.time is available on the classpath as the library under test.

I'm confirming the ISODateTimeFormat and DateTimeZone methods I need (dateTime, date, hourMinuteSecondMillis, dateHourMinuteSecondMillis, forOffsetHours, forOffsetMillis) exist in this joda-time version, and checking the LocalDate/LocalTime/LocalDateTime constructor signatures I'll need.

Now I'm writing out the test cases: covering the deprecated getChronology(), skipping the private constructor, confirming withZone's offsetParsed behavior, and verifying withLocale's null-equality short-circuit and equal-locale cases match the expected branches.

So to explicitly hit that equals-but-not-reference branch, I should construct two distinct Locale objects with equal value, like two separately created "en" locales, and verify withLocale returns the same instance since equals() holds true despite differing references. I'll apply similar separate-but-equal object reasoning for withChronology's reference check.

Since withZone and withChronology only check reference equality (no equals fallback), I only need tests confirming same-reference returns the original and different-reference always creates a new instance, which existing tests already cover. I'm now planning additional parseInto tests targeting the offsetParsed and zone-override branches before writing the final test file.

Then I verify that parsing with the explicit zone override forces the result into UTC regardless of the offset in the text, confirming millis stay at zero. I also note two more cases to cover: parseInto with a null instant should throw, and parseInto on invalid text should return a negative index rather than throwing.

Looking closer at the parseInto code, I notice it unconditionally calls bucket.computeMillis and sets the instant's millis even when the parse position comes back negative — there's no guard skipping that step on failure. So I can test this by parsing invalid text, asserting the returned position is negative, and still checking that the instant's millis got modified from its initial value despite the failure.

Now I need to design the full test cases: for the incomplete-parse scenario, I'll pick a formatter like dateHourMinuteSecondMillis with trailing extra characters in the text so the parse stops short of the full length and triggers the fallback IllegalArgumentException. I also need to account for ISODateTimeFormat.dateTime() requiring a mandatory offset suffix.

I'm planning to include direct tests for requirePrinter and requireParser exceptions using custom formatters built through the public constructor with one side null, then assemble the final code with a short explanatory table, double-checking that the DateTimeFormat method names I reference actually exist.

MutableDateTime implements ReadWritableInstant so it works with parseInto, unlike the immutable DateTime class. I'm also confirming that LocalDate, LocalTime, and LocalDateTime support equals comparisons for assertions, and that the ISODateTimeFormat static factory methods I'm relying on are accurate, along with DateTimeZone.forOffsetHours for fixed-offset zones.

I'm ready now to assemble the final file content along with a summary table mapping each test method to the branches and conditions it covers, keeping it concise given the size constraints.
